Fake Pandora Website UK: How to Spot & Avoid Jewellery Scam Sites

Fake Pandora sites copy the real jewellery brand and dangle big discounts — but you end up with counterfeit charms, nothing at all, or your card details in a scammer's hands.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-05-20 · Updated 2026-06-24 · 6 min read

fake Pandora website UKfake Pandora jewelleryPandora sale scam UKcounterfeit Pandora charmsPandora discount scam
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Report it — call Action Fraud on 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland: 101), and forward scam texts to 7726.

What is this scam?

Pandora is a well-known jewellery brand — charms, bracelets, rings and necklaces — with shops across the UK and an official website at pandora.net. A fake Pandora website scam involves criminals building lookalike sites that copy Pandora's branding, product photos and layout, then promote them through social media adverts, search results, or unsolicited texts and emails. The bait is almost always a dramatic discount: a 'closing down sale', 'clearance', or huge percentage off everything. The goal is to take your money for jewellery that is counterfeit or never arrives, to harvest your card and personal details, or both.

Because Pandora is so popular and its real products are widely recognised, a convincing fake storefront can catch out shoppers hunting for a bargain — especially around Christmas, Valentine's Day and Mother's Day when gift demand is high.

Warning signs to look for

  • The web address is not Pandora's official site. The genuine brand uses pandora.net (UK shoppers are served the UK store there); be wary of lookalikes such as 'pandora-uk-sale.com', 'pandoraoutlet.shop' or odd spellings designed to look official.
  • Discounts that are far below normal retail — site-wide '70% to 80% off', 'closing down' or 'liquidation' pricing on current designs.
  • The site is very new or has no verifiable company details: no UK registered address, no working contact route, or a contact page that only takes a web form.
  • You can only pay by bank transfer, cryptocurrency, or an unfamiliar payment page rather than a normal card checkout.
  • Pressure tactics such as countdown timers, 'only 2 left', or 'sale ends in 10 minutes' to rush you past your own judgement.
  • Poor English, mismatched fonts, or product images obviously copied from the real Pandora site.
  • Reviews appear only on the site itself, with nothing on independent review platforms — or the reviews look generic and over-positive.
  • The deal reached you through an unexpected social media advert, search result, text, or email rather than the official brand.

How this scam works step by step

You typically encounter the scam through a social media advert, a sponsored search result, or a text or email advertising a Pandora sale. The link takes you to a site that looks convincingly like the real Pandora store, complete with familiar charms and bracelets at steep discounts. You browse, pick a few items, and head to checkout. There you are asked for your card details and delivery information, and sometimes extra personal data.

From this point the scam plays out in one of a few ways: nothing is ever dispatched; a cheap counterfeit arrives instead of genuine Pandora; or your card details are used for further fraudulent charges or sold on. Some fake stores send a convincing 'order confirmed' or 'dispatched' email to keep you reassured and delay your suspicion until after the window for an easy refund or chargeback has passed.

How to verify if it is genuine

Before paying, check the web address yourself rather than trusting a link in an advert, text, or email. Open a new browser tab and type the official address — pandora.net — by hand, and confirm the exact spelling of the domain. Look for a genuine UK company address and a real contact route, and search the site's name alongside words like 'scam' or 'reviews' on independent platforms before you buy. Treat a discount that is far below normal retail as a warning sign in itself.

Wherever possible, pay by debit or credit card rather than bank transfer or cryptocurrency, because card payments keep you protected by chargeback (and, on credit-card purchases over £100, potentially Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act). If you are not sure a site is genuine, buy from a Pandora store or an established high-street retailer instead. For more on checking an unfamiliar shop, see our guide on how to tell if a website is a scam at Is This Website a Scam? A Practical Checklist Before You Buy.

What to do if you have already interacted

Act promptly if you have paid or entered details on a site you now doubt. If you paid by card, contact your bank or card provider straight away, report it, and ask about a chargeback or a Section 75 claim. If you paid by bank transfer, contact your bank immediately and ask about recovering an authorised push payment. Watch your statements for further charges and ask for a new card if your details may have been captured. If you reused the same password on the fake site that you use elsewhere, change it on those accounts.

If you handed over personal details such as your name, address or date of birth, stay alert for identity fraud: monitor your credit file with one of the three UK credit reference agencies — Experian, Equifax, or TransUnion — and consider a Cifas Protective Registration (cifas.org.uk), a paid marker that tells lenders to carry out extra identity checks before granting credit in your name. Keep evidence throughout: screenshots of the site, the web address, the advert or message, any emails, and the dates.

Reporting this scam in the UK

Report a fake Pandora website to Action Fraud, the UK's national fraud reporting centre, on 0300 123 2040 or at actionfraud.police.uk (in Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101). Forward phishing emails to the National Cyber Security Centre's Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk, and forward scam texts to 7726. If you received counterfeit goods or were misled by a trader, you can report the trader to Trading Standards through the Citizens Advice consumer helpline on 0808 223 1133.

Report the fake storefront to Pandora through the contact details on its official website so the brand can act to have it taken down, and if you have lost money, tell your bank as soon as possible. Keep copies of everything you report — it helps investigators link cases and warn other shoppers.

Frequently asked questions

Is Pandora a real company in the UK?

Yes. Pandora is a genuine, well-known jewellery brand with shops across the UK and an official website at pandora.net. That popularity is exactly why criminals copy it. The brand being real does not make every 'Pandora' website real, though — always confirm you are on the official site before you pay.

Why are the discounts on these sites so big?

Unusually deep discounts — 'closing down', 'liquidation', or a site-wide '80% off' — are the bait. Pandora and its authorised retailers run normal seasonal sales, not constant fire-sales on a brand-new web address. If a price looks far too good to be true, treat it as a warning sign and check the retailer carefully before paying.

I paid by card on a fake Pandora site — can I get my money back?

Possibly. Contact your card provider as soon as you can: card payments may be recoverable through chargeback, and credit-card purchases over £100 may be covered by Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act. Report it to Action Fraud as well. The sooner you act, the better your chances of recovering the money.

How do I find the real Pandora website?

Type the address into your browser yourself rather than clicking links in adverts, emails, or texts, and use the official pandora.net. If you are not sure a site is genuine, buy from a Pandora store or an established high-street retailer instead.
